W3-LO1 - Epidemiology and most common roots

Epidemiology

Explain the epidemiology of cervical nerve root compression and identify which cervical nerve roots have the highest frequency of being compressed.

Highest-yield frequency answer

For cervical radiculopathy, the course slide emphasizes lower cervical roots: C7 is most common, followed by C6. The lecture lists C7 around 70%, C6 around 20%, and C5/C8/T1 much less common.

PointCourse factHow it shows up in vignettes
AgeMean diagnosis age about 48; peak 50-54.Middle-aged patient with new arm pain, paresthesia, or reflex change.
Sex incidenceRochester cohort: higher incidence in men than women.Do not over-weight sex; root pattern and exam matter more.
Common cervical rootsC7 first, C6 second.C7: triceps/reflex/middle finger region. C6: biceps/brachioradialis/thumb-index region.
Lumbar rootsL5 and S1 are most commonly involved; L4-L5 and L5-S1 discs dominate.Leg symptoms often travel below the knee when a true root process is present.

Q: A 57-year-old has left arm pain, diminished triceps reflex, and Spurling reproduces symptoms. Which cervical root is most likely?

Answer

C7. C7 is the most frequent cervical radiculopathy root and classically maps to triceps reflex involvement.

W3-LO2 - Spinal root vs peripheral nerve

Localization

Differentiate and compare spinal nerve and peripheral nerve etiologies based on physical exams.

Localize before naming

A spinal nerve root problem usually has a myotomal, dermatomal, and reflex story. A peripheral nerve problem follows the named nerve's territory, often with sharper sensory borders and local entrapment signs.

Exam clueSpinal nerve/root etiologyPeripheral nerve etiology
Sensory patternReasonably dermatomal, but overlap is common; borders may be fuzzy.Named nerve distribution; sharp demarcation is more common.
Motor patternMyotomal weakness, often crossing more than one named peripheral nerve.Weakness limited to muscles supplied by one peripheral nerve.
ReflexesRoot-linked DTR can be decreased: biceps C5-6, brachioradialis C6, triceps C7, patellar L3-4, Achilles S1.Usually normal unless that reflex arc's peripheral nerve is directly involved.
ProvocationSpurling, SLR, cough/Valsalva, spine position can reproduce symptoms.Tinel/compression at tunnel, wrist/elbow/ankle position, local nerve stretch.
PalpationOften not reproducible by pressing superficial tissue over the pain area.May reproduce at entrapment site or trigger point.

Q: A patient has lateral thigh numbness only, no weakness, and risk factors of tight belt/tool belt use. Root or peripheral?

Answer

Peripheral nerve: lateral femoral cutaneous nerve entrapment, also called meralgia paresthetica, fits better than a lumbar root lesion.

W3-LO3 - Signs and symptoms of nerve irritation

Root Irritation Symptoms

Explain the signs and symptoms of spinal nerve irritation: pain, paresthesia, weakness.

Irritation vs failure

Pain and paresthesia can happen with irritation/inflammation before a root fails. Weakness, numbness, and reflex changes suggest conduction impairment and a truer radiculopathy.

Symptom/signMechanismExam question phrasing
PainChemical inflammation, ischemia, mechanical deformation, DRG sensitization.Sharp/electric pain radiating in a reasonably dermatomal pattern.
ParesthesiaSensory axon irritation.Tingling, pins/needles, burning, numbness in a root distribution.
WeaknessMotor conduction block or axonal compromise.Myotomal weakness: triceps, wrist extension, dorsiflexion, plantarflexion.
Reflex changeRoot-level disruption of reflex arc.Decreased DTR points toward the involved root; hyperreflexia points to cord/UMN.
Position sensitivityForaminal narrowing or dural/root tension.Worse with neck extension/rotation, cough, Valsalva, SLR, standing/walking in stenosis.

Q: What is the clinical meaning of pain and paresthesia without objective weakness/reflex change?

Answer

That pattern is often described as radiculitis: irritated/inflamed nerve root without clear conduction loss.

W3-LO4 - Radiculitis, radiculopathy, myelopathy

Definitions

Differentiate between radiculitis, radiculopathy, and myelopathy.

TermDefinitionPatternWhat not to miss
RadiculitisInflammation/irritation of a spinal nerve root.Pain/paresthesia, often without objective motor/reflex deficit.Can be chemical from annular tear or disc inflammation.
RadiculopathyDisease of a spinal nerve root with conduction block/interruption.Pain plus objective sensory, motor, or reflex findings.Progressive deficit escalates the plan.
MyelopathySpinal cord dysfunction.UMN signs: gait change, spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, Babinski/Hoffman, hand clumsiness.Cord signs require urgent imaging/referral.
Peripheral neuropathyDisease of peripheral nerves.Named nerve or stocking-glove pattern.Do not call stocking-glove loss a single root lesion.

Q: A patient with neck pain has wide-based gait, clonus, and positive Hoffman's sign. Why is this not a routine radiculopathy visit?

Answer

Those are upper motor neuron/myelopathy signs, meaning possible cord compression. This needs urgent imaging and specialty evaluation.

W3-LO5 - Spondylosis and spondyloarthropathy

Degenerative vs Inflammatory

Define and explain the pathophysiology of spondylosis and spondyloarthropathy.

Spondylosis

Spondylosis is degenerative spine change: disc desiccation/height loss, endplate change, facet/uncovertebral hypertrophy, ligament thickening, and osteophyte formation. It narrows canals/foramina mechanically and can add inflammation.

Spondyloarthropathy

Spondyloarthropathy is inflammatory/autoimmune axial or enthesis disease, classically including ankylosing spondylitis and related conditions. The story is inflammatory back pain, stiffness, systemic clues, or SI involvement, not a single mechanical root.

FeatureSpondylosisSpondyloarthropathy
Core processWear/degenerative remodeling.Immune-mediated inflammation at joints/entheses.
Pain patternMechanical; worse with loading/extension; may cause radic if foramina narrow.Inflammatory; morning stiffness, improves with movement/exercise.
Imaging ideaDisc height loss, osteophytes, facet arthropathy, stenosis.Sacroiliitis, syndesmophytes, inflammatory erosive/fusion patterns depending on disease.
OMT thoughtGentle OMT may help compensatory somatic dysfunction if no red flags/instability.Use caution in severe/fused disease; avoid aggressive techniques when fracture/instability risk is elevated.

Q: A vignette says degenerative disc height loss, uncovertebral osteophytes, and foraminal narrowing. What umbrella term is being described?

Answer

Spondylosis, which can mechanically compress roots through bony and disc-related narrowing.

W3-LO6 - Cervical and lumbar differential map

Differential Diagnosis

Compare, contrast, explain, and identify cervical and lumbar findings including stenosis, disc herniation, spondylosis, spondylolysis, spondylolisthesis, spondyloarthropathy, psoas syndrome, piriformis syndrome, bursitis, and cauda equina syndrome.

Vignette approach

First decide: root, cord, local spine pain, hip/SI, muscle/tenderpoint, peripheral nerve, vascular, infection/malignancy, or emergent cauda equina. Then match imaging and exam clues.

ConditionDefinition/pathophysSymptoms/vignette cluePicture/imaging clue
Cervical/lumbar disc herniationNucleus pulposus protrudes through annulus; chemical and mechanical root irritation.Acute or gradual radicular pain; cough/Valsalva may worsen; lumbar SLR positive.MRI shows protrusion/extrusion; posterolateral lower lumbar catches traversing root.
Spinal stenosisCentral canal/lateral recess narrowing from disc, facet, and ligamentous hypertrophy.Neurogenic claudication: worse standing/walking, better sitting/flexion/grocery cart.Central canal narrowing on MRI/CT; severe cases risk cauda equina.
SpondylosisDegenerative bony/disc change.Mechanical neck/back pain, foraminal narrowing, older patient.Osteophytes, disc height loss, facet/uncovertebral arthropathy.
SpondylolysisPars interarticularis stress defect/fracture.Extension-related low back pain; athlete/adolescent possible."Scottie dog collar" on oblique x-ray.
SpondylolisthesisVertebral slippage after pars defect or degenerative instability.Back pain, possible foraminal stenosis/radic; palpable step-off.Lateral x-ray shows anterior or posterior slip; flexion/extension films assess motion.
SpondyloarthropathyInflammatory axial/enthesis disease.Morning stiffness better with exercise, SI pain, uveitis/psoriasis/IBD clue.Sacroiliitis or syndesmophytes, not a simple disc picture.
Psoas syndromeIliopsoas hypertonicity/tenderpoint; can accompany upper lumbar disc disease.Hip flexion posture, anterior thigh/hip pain, reduced hip extension.Usually clinical; consider MRI if upper lumbar radic signs coexist.
Piriformis syndromeSciatic nerve irritation under/through piriformis.Buttock pain radiating posterior/lateral leg; palpation over piriformis reproduces.Usually clinical; normal spine neuroimaging does not exclude it.
BursitisTrochanteric or ischial bursal inflammation.Focal tenderness over greater trochanter or ischial tuberosity; may radiate but usually not past knee.Clinical or ultrasound/MRI if uncertain.
Cauda equina syndromeCompression of lumbosacral nerve roots below conus.Saddle anesthesia, urinary retention/incontinence, bowel dysfunction, bilateral symptoms, severe weakness.Urgent MRI; surgical decompression pathway.

Q: A patient can walk only short distances, then must sit; leaning over a cart helps. Most likely diagnosis?

Answer

Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication. Flexion opens the canal/foramina; extension and standing narrow them.

W3-LO7 - Pain generator differentiation

Pain Pattern Discrimination

Differentiate discogenic pain, facet joint pain, myofascial pain, and radicular pain.

Pain generatorPatternProvoked byNeurologic deficits?Palpation clue
DiscogenicDeep axial back pain, may refer into buttock/thigh; annular tears can cause chemical radiculitis.Sitting, flexion, Valsalva/cough in some disc cases.Not necessarily unless root involved.Disc itself is not reproduced by superficial palpation.
Facet jointAxial neck/back with referral; lumbar may mimic hip/SI.Extension, rotation, facet loading/Kemp's.No objective root deficit expected.Posterior element/facet tenderness can reproduce local/referral pain.
MyofascialTrigger-point referral that may look radicular.Muscle load, posture, direct trigger-point pressure.No myotomal/reflex deficit.Palpable hyperirritable nodule reproduces the complaint.
RadicularReasonably dermatomal pain/paresthesia; often distal, below knee for lumbar.Spine position, SLR, Spurling, cough/Valsalva.May have weakness, sensory loss, or reduced DTR.Usually not reproduced by pressing a superficial trigger point alone.

Q: A low back pain patient has pain to the lateral thigh, normal reflexes/strength, and exquisite tenderness over the greater trochanter. What pain generator wins?

Answer

Trochanteric bursitis/greater trochanteric pain syndrome is more likely than radiculopathy because the focal palpation finding and normal neuro exam dominate.

W3-LO8 - Cauda equina syndrome

Emergency Syndrome

Define and explain the pathophysiology of cauda equina syndrome.

Cauda equina is a same-day emergency

Cauda equina syndrome occurs when multiple lumbosacral nerve roots are compressed in the canal, classically by a large central disc herniation, severe stenosis, tumor, infection, hematoma, or trauma. Root compression affects bladder, bowel, saddle sensation, sexual function, and leg motor/sensory function.

Root bundle functionClinical manifestation when compressed
S2-S4 parasympathetic fibersUrinary retention or overflow incontinence; bowel dysfunction.
S2-S5 sensory rootsSaddle anesthesia/perineal sensory loss.
Lumbosacral motor rootsBilateral weakness, gait difficulty, reduced reflexes depending on level.
Mixed roots in canalBilateral sciatica or rapidly progressive neurologic deficit.

Q: Which symptom in a radicular low back patient is most concerning for cauda equina syndrome?

Answer

New urinary retention, especially with saddle anesthesia, bowel dysfunction, bilateral leg symptoms, or progressive weakness.

W3-LO9 - Clinical management

Management

Explain the clinical management of patients with radicular complaints.

Management sequence

Start with triage: red flags first. If none, treat pain/function conservatively, reassess neurologic status, and escalate for progressive deficit or persistent disabling symptoms.

  1. Screen for emergency/red flags. Ask about bowel/bladder dysfunction, saddle anesthesia, fever, cancer, immunosuppression, IV drug use, trauma, progressive weakness, myelopathic signs, and severe unrelenting night/rest pain.
  2. Localize clinically. History plus strength, sensation, DTRs, special tests, gait, and osteopathic structural exam.
  3. Initial conservative plan if uncomplicated. Education, stay active, avoid bed rest beyond brief comfort, NSAIDs/acetaminophen as appropriate, short course muscle relaxant or neuropathic agent when appropriate, PT/home exercise, and close follow-up.
  4. Target inflammation/pain when selected. Course management includes glucocorticoids, NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors, ketorolac, tramadol/opioids selectively, gabapentin/pregabalin, TCA/SNRI, and fluoroscopic epidural steroid injection for selected radicular pain.
  5. Use OMT thoughtfully. Prefer gentle indirect, soft tissue, counterstrain, FPR, BLT, traction/decompression-style approaches when tolerated; avoid aggressive direct techniques in acute neurologic compromise.
  6. Escalate. MRI/referral for red flags, progressive objective deficit, myelopathy, suspected cauda equina, infection/malignancy, or persistent symptoms after a reasonable conservative trial.

Q: In uncomplicated acute low back pain with radicular symptoms but no red flags, what should you avoid prescribing as the main treatment?

Answer

Avoid prolonged bed rest. Course slide: bed rest over 2 days is bad; education and activity are favored.

W3-LO10 - Red flags

Red Flags

Explain, list, and identify red flags associated with radicular patterns that would prompt immediate attention and further workup.

Immediate attention/red flag list

  • Cauda equina: saddle anesthesia, urinary retention/incontinence, bowel dysfunction, bilateral severe symptoms.
  • Progressive neurologic deficit: worsening weakness, atrophy, inability to heel/toe walk, inability to squat and rise.
  • Myelopathy/UMN: gait abnormality, spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, Babinski, Hoffman's, Lhermitte's, fine motor decline.
  • Infection/tumor: fever, chills, weight loss, night/rest pain, immunosuppression, cancer history, IV drug use.
  • Trauma/fracture/instability: significant trauma, osteoporosis/steroid risk, protruding deformity or step-off, focal vertebral tenderness.
  • Non-spine emergencies: abdominal pain, dyspnea, vascular symptoms, or pain pattern that does not match spine mechanics.

Q: A radicular complaint plus clumsy gait and hyperreflexia should trigger what next step?

Answer

Urgent evaluation for myelopathy, usually MRI and neurosurgical/spine consultation depending on setting and severity.

W3-LO11 - Imaging

Imaging and Studies

Explain and identify indications for and types of imaging most appropriate for a patient with radiculopathy.

Do not image every radic immediately

For uncomplicated acute low back pain/radiculopathy without red flags, major guidelines generally avoid immediate imaging. Image early when red flags or progressive neurologic deficits are present, or when symptoms persist despite a conservative trial and an intervention/surgical pathway is being considered.

StudyBest useCourse pearl
X-rayTrauma, suspected fracture, degeneration overview, alignment, instability screening.Flexion-extension views help assess dynamic instability; oblique views can show foraminal narrowing/spondylosis.
MRI without contrastPreferred for disc herniation, stenosis, nerve root compression, myelopathy, most nontraumatic radiculopathy when imaging is indicated.Clinical correlation is mandatory because degenerative findings are common in asymptomatic patients.
MRI with contrastConcern for cancer/infection, postoperative scar vs recurrent disc, inflammatory or mass process.Course slide: use contrast if cancer is on DDx or history of prior spinal surgery.
CTBony detail, acute trauma, when MRI unavailable/contraindicated.Excellent bone detail; weaker soft tissue/root visualization than MRI.
CT myelogramWhen MRI is contraindicated/equivocal or to clarify clinically apparent root impingement.Dye cutoff/blunting can identify an affected root sleeve.
EMG/NCSUnclear localization, chronicity, or distinguishing root lesion from peripheral neuropathy.NCS alone is not enough for radiculopathy; needle EMG adds root-level information.

Q: When is MRI especially appropriate in suspected radiculopathy?

Answer

When there are red flags, suspected myelopathy/cauda equina/infection/malignancy, progressive objective neurologic deficit, or persistent symptoms after conservative care when injection/surgery is being considered.

W3-LO12 - OMT indications and contraindications

OMT Safety

Explain and identify indications and contraindications for OMT in patients with radicular symptoms.

OMT situationIndicated?Reasoning
Somatic dysfunction with mild stable radicular symptoms and normal neuro examOften yes, with cautionGentle indirect/soft tissue/traction-style care may reduce nociception and improve mechanics.
Acute severe radicular pain but no progressive deficitSelective and gentleUse pain-free positions; avoid compressing into symptoms.
Progressive weakness, bowel/bladder symptoms, saddle anesthesiaNo routine OMT firstEmergency workup/referral is priority.
Myelopathy signs: hyperreflexia, clonus, Babinski, gait disturbanceContraindication to aggressive OMTPossible cord compression needs imaging and specialty management.
Fracture, malignancy, infection, severe osteoporosis, instabilityContraindicated or heavily modifiedRisk of harm exceeds benefit until clarified/managed.
Prior spine surgery/fusion/hardwareRequires history/imaging contextConfirm stability and choose gentle non-thrust techniques around, not through, vulnerable segments.
Radicular symptoms are not a license for thrust

Direct cervical or lumbar thrust is inappropriate when neurologic status is changing, cord signs are present, or structural stability is uncertain. The course cases repeatedly route red flags to imaging before OMT.

Q: A patient has neck pain and a positive Hoffman's sign. Should you perform cervical HVLA before imaging?

Answer

No. Positive Hoffman's suggests an upper motor neuron process/myelopathy risk. Escalate to imaging/specialty evaluation.

W3-LO13 - OMT application

OMT Application

Explain and apply the appropriate application of OMT to a patient with radicular complaints.

OMT goal in radicular complaints

Treat what is safe and treatable: secondary somatic dysfunction, muscle guarding, tenderpoints, fascial/ligamentous tension, and mechanics that aggravate foraminal load. Do not claim OMT is decompressing a surgical emergency.

  1. Triage and consent. Confirm no red flags; explain that treatment will stop if symptoms peripheralize or neurologic symptoms worsen.
  2. Establish baseline. Document pain distribution, strength, sensation, DTRs, provocative tests, gait, and relevant osteopathic findings.
  3. Choose low-risk technique first. Soft tissue, counterstrain, FPR, BLT, gentle ME, and traction/decompression positions are safer first choices than aggressive direct methods.
  4. Prefer centralization/ease. Use positions that reduce distal symptoms. Stop if symptoms worsen or spread distally.
  5. Treat related regions. For cervical radic: thoracic outlet, ribs, scalenes, upper thoracic, OA/AA if safe. For lumbar radic: pelvis/sacrum, psoas/piriformis, lumbar paraspinals, nerve-root decompression-style FPR.
  6. Recheck and safety-net. Repeat neurologic screen if symptoms changed; document response and give clear red-flag return instructions.
ComplaintReasonable OMT targetsAvoid/caution
Cervical radicular patternThoracic inlet/outlet, rib mechanics, scalenes/anterior cervical tenderpoints, OA/AA/lower cervical only if no red flags.Cervical thrust or compression into Spurling-like position if symptoms worsen.
Lumbar radicular patternPsoas, piriformis, sacrum/pelvis, lumbar paraspinals, gentle traction/FPR nerve-root setup.Compression that peripheralizes pain; lumbar HVLA with progressive neurologic deficit.
Myofascial mimicCounterstrain, soft tissue, ME, stretching, postural/load correction.Overcalling as disc disease if palpation fully reproduces pain and neuro exam is normal.

Q: During lumbar FPR/traction-style treatment, leg pain moves farther down the leg. What should you do?

Answer

Stop or modify. Worsening/peripheralization means the position or force is not appropriate; reassess neurologic status and the diagnosis.

W3-LO14 - Specialized tests

Special Tests

Explain and identify Spurling's Maneuver, Lhermitte's Sign, Straight Leg Raising Test, step-off deformity evaluation, lumbar spinous process percussion, Hoffman's Sign, clonus/hyperreflexia testing, and Babinski Sign.

Test/signHow to performPositive findingMeaning
Spurling's maneuverExtend/sidebend/rotate neck toward symptomatic side; gentle axial compression.Ipsilateral arm radicular pain/paresthesia.Specific confirmatory test for cervical radiculopathy.
Lhermitte's signFlex the neck.Electric shock sensation down spine or into limbs.Central cord/dorsal column irritation: myelopathy, MS, tumor, B12, whiplash contexts.
Straight leg raiseSupine passive hip flexion with knee extended; sensitizer with ankle dorsiflexion.Radicular leg pain, classically below knee, often 30-70 degrees.Lumbosacral nerve root/dural tension, often disc herniation.
Crossed SLRRaise asymptomatic leg.Pain in symptomatic leg.More specific for disc herniation.
Step-off deformityPalpate lumbar spinous processes for abrupt anterior/posterior offset.Palpable drop/step.Spondylolisthesis/instability clue.
Lumbar spinous percussionGently percuss spinous processes or axial skeleton when fracture/infection/malignancy is possible.Focal bony pain.Vertebral fracture, infection, or malignancy concern; image if clinically appropriate.
Hoffman's signFlick/nip distal middle finger nail.Thumb/index flexion or finger flexion response.Upper motor neuron sign; screen for cervical myelopathy.
Clonus/hyperreflexiaRapid ankle dorsiflexion for clonus; compare DTRs bilaterally.Sustained beats or generalized brisk reflexes.UMN/cord process until proven otherwise.
Babinski signStroke lateral plantar foot from heel to forefoot, then medially.Great toe dorsiflexion/fanning.UMN sign.
Kemp's testLumbar extension, sidebending, rotation with axial load.Local facet pain or radicular pain depending on response.Facet loading; may also provoke foraminal/root symptoms.

Q: Which special-test result turns a radicular neck complaint into a cord-workup problem?

Answer

Lhermitte's, Hoffman's, clonus, hyperreflexia, Babinski, gait disturbance, or fine motor decline. These point to myelopathy/UMN involvement.

W3-LO15 - Technique identification and application

OMT Technique Recognition

Explain, demonstrate knowledge, and identify Still, Counterstrain, FPR, and ME techniques for Type 1 and Type 2 dysfunctions and tissue texture changes involving OA, AA, lower cervical, lumbar, sacrum, anterior cervical/lumbar tenderpoints, psoas tenderpoints, and lumbar nerve-root decompression.

Technique ID shortcuts

Still: start in ease, add compression/traction, move through neutral toward barrier. FPR: neutral/idling, add facilitating force, move into ease, hold seconds. Counterstrain: tenderpoint, position of comfort, tenderness drops. Muscle Energy (ME): physician engages barrier, patient gives isometric contraction, relax, take up slack, repeat.

Region/problemStill/FPR/CS/ME applicationBoard-style recognition phrase
OA Type 2 dysfunctionStill can treat OA by positioning occiput into ease, adding compression, then moving toward the barrier; ME often uses eye/cranial or head motion into barrier with gentle isometric contraction.OA named by occiput on atlas: e.g., OA ESrRl or OA FSlRr.
AA dysfunctionAA is primarily rotation. Still starts rotated into ease, compresses, then rotates through barrier. ME engages rotational barrier and patient gently rotates opposite physician resistance.AA Rr/AA Rl; about half cervical rotation occurs here.
Lower cervical Type 2Still: ease in rotation/sidebending plus flexion/extension component, compress, then move opposite while localizing. FPR: flex to neutral/idling, compress, then position ease. ME: barrier in all planes, 3-5 sec contraction, repeat.Lower cervical mechanics: Type 2 rotation and sidebending same side.
Seated lumbar Type 1Still seated: stand behind, localize curve, exaggerate ease, compress through shoulders/torso, reverse sidebending/rotation.Neutral dysfunction: group curve, rotation and sidebending opposite.
Supine lumbar Type 1Use hip/knee flexion and leg arc to exaggerate curve, add compression/traction, sweep through barrier.Leg position controls lumbar sidebending/rotation.
Supine lumbar Type 2 flexedStand on posterior TP side; knee over segment; adduct to ease for flexed dysfunction, compress, abduct and extend back to neutral.Flexed Type 2: start with leg adducted if that gives ease.
Supine lumbar Type 2 extendedStand on posterior TP side; abduct to ease for extended dysfunction, compress, adduct and extend back to neutral.Extended Type 2: start with leg abducted if that gives ease.
Sacrum/lumbar regionStill sacrum uses ipsilateral hip flexion to sacral engagement, finds adduction/abduction ease, compresses through knee, arcs toward restriction.Monitoring hand at SI/sacrum; lower extremity creates sacral motion.
Anterior cervical tenderpointsCounterstrain AC2-6 generally uses flexion to segment with sidebend away and rotate away from tenderpoint.AC points follow SARA: sidebend away, rotate away.
Anterior lumbar tenderpointsCounterstrain AL3/AL4 around AIIS; flex hips to level and sidebend/rotate away. AL5 near pubic ramus, marked hip flexion with rotation toward and sidebend away.Tenderpoint location drives position of comfort.
Psoas tenderpointCounterstrain: marked hip flexion, knees flexed, crossed ankles, hips externally rotated, slight ipsilateral sidebending.Anterior hip/thigh or thoracolumbar pain with reduced hip extension.
Piriformis tenderpointCounterstrain: prone, hip flexed around 90 degrees and markedly abducted; fine-tune rotation.Buttock tenderpoint midway between greater trochanter and coccyx/PSIS line.
Lumbar nerve-root decompressionFPR-style: prone with abdomen pillow, affected leg off table, hip/knee flexed, abduct/flex/compress-shortening or traction/gapping, hold 4-5 sec and repeat.Course slide names this as FPR for lumbar nerve-root pain.

Q: A vignette says: diagnose L4 ESRl, place the patient's hip abducted until ease is felt, add compression, then adduct and extend the leg. Which technique?

Answer

Still technique for an extended lumbar Type 2 dysfunction. Ease first, compression, then an arc toward the barrier.

Week 3 OMM - High-Yield One-Pager

Condensed by learning objective. Use this after the full pass.

LO1

Cervical: C7 most common (~70%), then C6 (~20%); C5/C8/T1 rare. C7 → triceps reflex/middle finger. C6 → biceps/brachioradialis/thumb-index. Mean age ~48, peak 50-54; more common in men.
Lumbar: L5 and S1 most common; L4-L5 and L5-S1 discs dominate. Posterolateral herniation hits the traversing root (below disc level); far-lateral hits the exiting root.

LO2

Root/spinal nerve: myotomal weakness crossing >1 peripheral nerve, dermatomal sensory loss with fuzzy borders, root-linked DTR loss (biceps C5-6, brachioradialis C6, triceps C7, patellar L3-4, Achilles S1), reproduced by Spurling/SLR/cough/Valsalva; palpation over the painful area is usually not reproducible.
Peripheral nerve: weakness limited to that nerve's muscles, sharp sensory border along a named territory, normal reflexes unless that arc is involved, reproduced by Tinel/compression/stretch at the entrapment site.

LO3

Pain: chemical inflammation, ischemia, mechanical deformation, DRG sensitization → sharp/electric, dermatomal.
Paresthesia: sensory axon irritation → tingling/burning/numbness in a root distribution.
Weakness: motor conduction block/axonal compromise → myotomal (triceps, wrist extension, dorsiflexion, plantarflexion).
Reflex change: decreased DTR = root level; hyperreflexia = cord/UMN. Pain/paresthesia with no objective weakness or reflex loss = radiculitis.

LO4

Radiculitis = inflamed/irritated root; pain/paresthesia, usually no objective deficit.
Radiculopathy = root disease with conduction block; pain plus objective sensory, motor, or reflex findings.
Myelopathy = spinal cord dysfunction; UMN signs — gait change, spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, Babinski/Hoffman's, hand clumsiness; needs urgent imaging/referral.
Peripheral neuropathy = named-nerve or stocking-glove pattern, not a single root.

LO5

Spondylosis = degenerative: disc desiccation/height loss, endplate change, facet/uncovertebral hypertrophy, ligament thickening, osteophytes → mechanically narrows canal/foramina; mechanical pain worse with loading/extension.
Spondyloarthropathy = inflammatory/autoimmune axial/enthesis disease (e.g., ankylosing spondylitis); morning stiffness that improves with movement, SI involvement, systemic clues (uveitis/psoriasis/IBD); imaging shows sacroiliitis/syndesmophytes, not a disc picture. OMT: gentle for spondylosis if no red flags; caution/avoid aggressive technique in fused or unstable spondyloarthropathy.

LO6

First localize: root, cord, local spine pain, hip/SI, muscle/tenderpoint, peripheral nerve, vascular, infection/malignancy, or emergent cauda equina — then match imaging/exam clues. Full ten-condition differential table is below (disc herniation, stenosis, spondylosis, spondylolysis, spondylolisthesis, spondyloarthropathy, psoas syndrome, piriformis syndrome, bursitis, cauda equina).

LO7

Discogenic: deep axial pain, may refer to buttock/thigh; provoked by sitting/flexion/Valsalva.
Facet joint: axial pain with referral (lumbar can mimic hip/SI); provoked by extension/rotation/Kemp's; no objective root deficit.
Myofascial: trigger-point referral that can mimic radicular pain; reproduced by direct trigger-point pressure; no myotomal/reflex deficit.
Radicular: dermatomal pain/paresthesia, often distal (below knee for lumbar); provoked by spine position, SLR, Spurling, cough/Valsalva; may show weakness, sensory loss, or reduced DTR.

LO8

Compression of multiple lumbosacral nerve roots in the canal — classically a large central disc herniation, severe stenosis, tumor, infection, hematoma, or trauma.
S2-S4 parasympathetic: urinary retention/overflow incontinence, bowel dysfunction.
S2-S5 sensory: saddle anesthesia/perineal loss.
Lumbosacral motor roots: bilateral weakness, gait difficulty, reduced reflexes.
Most concerning single symptom: new urinary retention. This is a same-day surgical emergency.

LO9

1. Triage red flags first (bowel/bladder, saddle anesthesia, fever/cancer/immunosuppression/IVDU, trauma, progressive weakness, myelopathic signs, unrelenting night pain).
2. Localize clinically: strength, sensation, DTRs, special tests, gait, OMM structural exam.
3. Conservative if uncomplicated: education, stay active, avoid bed rest >2 days, NSAIDs/acetaminophen, short-course muscle relaxant or neuropathic agent, PT/home exercise, close follow-up.
4. Selected pain control: glucocorticoids, NSAIDs/COX-2, ketorolac, tramadol/opioids selectively, gabapentin/pregabalin, TCA/SNRI, fluoroscopic epidural steroid injection.
5. OMT thoughtfully — gentle indirect/soft tissue/CS/FPR/BLT/traction; avoid aggressive direct technique in acute neuro compromise.
6. Escalate for red flags, progressive deficit, myelopathy, cauda equina, infection/malignancy, or a failed conservative trial.

LO10

Cauda equina: saddle anesthesia, urinary retention/incontinence, bowel dysfunction, bilateral severe symptoms.
Progressive deficit: worsening weakness, atrophy, can't heel/toe walk or squat-and-rise.
Myelopathy/UMN: gait abnormality, spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, Babinski, Hoffman's, Lhermitte's, fine motor decline.
Infection/tumor: fever, chills, weight loss, night/rest pain, immunosuppression, cancer history, IVDU.
Trauma/instability: significant trauma, osteoporosis/steroid use, step-off deformity, focal vertebral tenderness.
Non-spine emergency: abdominal pain, dyspnea, vascular symptoms, mechanics-mismatched pain.

LO11

Do not image every uncomplicated acute radic case without red flags. Image early for red flags, progressive deficit, or persistent symptoms when intervention is being considered.
X-ray: trauma, fracture, alignment/instability (flexion-extension views), oblique for foraminal narrowing.
MRI w/o contrast: preferred for disc herniation, stenosis, root compression, myelopathy — most nontraumatic radiculopathy; correlate clinically since degenerative findings are common in asymptomatic patients.
MRI w/ contrast: cancer/infection concern, postop scar vs. recurrent disc, inflammatory/mass process.
CT: bony detail, acute trauma, MRI unavailable/contraindicated.
CT myelogram: MRI contraindicated/equivocal, or to clarify root impingement.
EMG/NCS: unclear localization/chronicity or root vs. peripheral neuropathy; needle EMG adds root-level info beyond NCS alone.

LO12

OMT is appropriate for stable somatic dysfunction with mild, non-progressive radicular symptoms and a normal neuro exam. It is not a substitute for emergency workup when progressive deficit, bowel/bladder change, saddle anesthesia, myelopathy signs, fracture, malignancy, infection, severe osteoporosis, or instability are present. Full indications/contraindications table is below.

LO13

Goal: treat what's safe/treatable — secondary somatic dysfunction, muscle guarding, tenderpoints, fascial/ligamentous tension, mechanics aggravating foraminal load. OMT does not decompress a surgical emergency.
Sequence: triage/consent (stop if symptoms peripheralize) → baseline exam (pain distribution, strength, sensation, DTRs, provocative tests, gait, structural exam) → low-risk technique first (soft tissue, counterstrain, FPR, BLT, gentle ME, traction/decompression) → prefer centralization/ease, stop if symptoms worsen/spread distally → treat related regions (cervical: thoracic outlet, ribs, scalenes, upper thoracic, OA/AA if safe; lumbar: pelvis/sacrum, psoas/piriformis, paraspinals, nerve-root decompression FPR) → recheck neuro status and give safety-net instructions. Avoid cervical thrust/compression into a Spurling-like position or lumbar HVLA that peripheralizes pain with any progressive deficit.

LO14

Eight named tests to recognize by vignette: Spurling's, Lhermitte's, straight leg raise, step-off deformity, lumbar spinous percussion, Hoffman's, clonus/hyperreflexia, and Babinski. Spurling and SLR confirm root tension; Lhermitte's/Hoffman's/clonus/Babinski are cord/UMN red flags; step-off and percussion screen for instability/fracture/infection. Full how-to-perform and meaning table is below.

LO15

Still = position into ease → add compression/traction → move through neutral toward the barrier.
FPR = neutral/idle position → add facilitating force → move into ease, hold seconds.
Counterstrain = find tenderpoint → position of comfort until tenderness drops.
Muscle Energy (ME) = engage barrier → isometric contraction → relax → take up slack, repeat.
Full region-by-region atlas (OA, AA, lower cervical, seated/supine lumbar Type 1 & 2, sacrum, anterior cervical/lumbar tenderpoints, psoas, piriformis, lumbar nerve-root decompression) is below.

LO6 — Cervical/Lumbar Differential Map

ConditionKey finding / symptomImaging or exam clue
Cervical/lumbar disc herniationAcute or gradual radicular pain; cough/Valsalva worsens; lumbar SLR positiveMRI: protrusion/extrusion; posterolateral catches traversing root
Spinal stenosisNeurogenic claudication — worse standing/walking, better sitting/flexion ("grocery cart" sign)Central canal narrowing on MRI/CT; severe cases risk cauda equina
SpondylosisMechanical neck/back pain, foraminal narrowing, older patientOsteophytes, disc height loss, facet/uncovertebral arthropathy
SpondylolysisExtension-related low back pain; athlete/adolescent"Scottie dog collar" fracture on oblique x-ray
SpondylolisthesisBack pain, possible foraminal stenosis/radic; palpable step-offLateral x-ray shows anterior/posterior slip; flexion-extension films assess motion
SpondyloarthropathyMorning stiffness, better with exercise, SI pain, uveitis/psoriasis/IBD clueSacroiliitis or syndesmophytes, not a simple disc picture
Psoas syndromeHip flexion posture, anterior thigh/hip pain, reduced hip extensionUsually clinical; consider MRI if upper lumbar radic signs coexist
Piriformis syndromeButtock pain radiating posterior/lateral leg; palpation over piriformis reproducesUsually clinical; normal spine imaging does not exclude it
Bursitis (trochanteric/ischial)Focal tenderness over trochanter/ischial tuberosity; usually not past kneeClinical or ultrasound/MRI if uncertain
Cauda equina syndromeSaddle anesthesia, urinary retention/incontinence, bowel dysfunction, bilateral symptoms, severe weaknessUrgent MRI; surgical decompression pathway

LO14 — Special Tests

Test/signHow to performPositive findingMeaning
Spurling's maneuverExtend/sidebend/rotate neck toward symptomatic side; gentle axial compressionIpsilateral arm radicular pain/paresthesiaConfirms cervical radiculopathy
Lhermitte's signFlex the neckElectric shock sensation down spine or into limbsCord/dorsal column irritation: myelopathy, MS, tumor, B12, whiplash
Straight leg raise (SLR)Supine passive hip flexion with knee extended; ankle dorsiflexion sensitizesRadicular leg pain, classically below knee, often 30-70 degreesLumbosacral nerve root/dural tension, often disc herniation
Crossed SLRRaise the asymptomatic legPain in the symptomatic legMore specific for disc herniation
Step-off deformityPalpate lumbar spinous processes for abrupt anterior/posterior offsetPalpable drop/stepSpondylolisthesis/instability clue
Lumbar spinous process percussionGently percuss spinous processes/axial skeleton when fracture/infection/malignancy possibleFocal bony painVertebral fracture, infection, or malignancy concern
Hoffman's signFlick/nip the distal middle fingernailThumb/index finger flexion responseUMN sign; screen for cervical myelopathy
Clonus / hyperreflexiaRapid ankle dorsiflexion for clonus; compare DTRs bilaterallySustained beats or generalized brisk reflexesUMN/cord process until proven otherwise
Babinski signStroke lateral plantar foot from heel to forefoot, then mediallyGreat toe dorsiflexion/fanningUMN sign

LO15 — Technique Atlas by Region/Dysfunction

Region / dysfunctionTechnique & setupRecognition phrase
OA Type 2Still: position occiput into ease, add compression/traction, move toward barrier. ME: head motion into barrier with gentle isometric contraction.Named by occiput-on-atlas, e.g. OA ESrRl or OA FSlRr
AA dysfunction (rotation)Still: rotate into ease, compress, rotate through barrier. ME: engage rotational barrier, patient gently rotates against resistance.AA Rr / AA Rl; about half of cervical rotation occurs here
Lower cervical Type 2Still: ease in rotation/sidebending plus flexion/extension, compress, move opposite while localizing. FPR: flex to neutral/idling, compress, position of ease. ME: engage barrier in all planes, 3-5 sec contraction, repeat.Type 2 = rotation and sidebending same side
Seated lumbar Type 1Still: stand behind, localize the curve, exaggerate ease, compress through shoulders/torso, reverse sidebending/rotation.Group curve: rotation and sidebending opposite
Supine lumbar Type 1Use hip/knee flexion and leg arc to exaggerate the curve, add compression/traction, sweep through the barrier.Leg position controls lumbar sidebending/rotation
Supine lumbar Type 2 (flexed)Stand on posterior transverse-process side, knee over segment, adduct to ease, compress, then abduct/extend to neutral.Flexed Type 2: start with leg adducted if that gives ease
Supine lumbar Type 2 (extended)Stand on posterior TP side, abduct to ease, compress, then adduct/extend to neutral.Extended Type 2: start with leg abducted if that gives ease
Sacrum / lumbar regionStill: ipsilateral hip flexion to sacral engagement, find adduction/abduction ease, compress through knee, arc toward restriction.Monitor at SI/sacrum; lower extremity creates sacral motion
Anterior cervical tenderpoints (AC2-6)Counterstrain: flex to segment, sidebend away and rotate away from the tenderpoint.Follows SARA: sidebend away, rotate away
Anterior lumbar tenderpoints (AL3-5)Counterstrain: AL3/AL4 near AIIS — flex hips to level, sidebend/rotate away. AL5 near pubic ramus — marked hip flexion, rotate toward, sidebend away.Tenderpoint location drives the position of comfort
Psoas tenderpointCounterstrain: marked hip flexion, knees flexed, ankles crossed, hips externally rotated, slight ipsilateral sidebending.Anterior hip/thigh or thoracolumbar pain, reduced hip extension
Piriformis tenderpointCounterstrain: prone, hip flexed ~90 degrees and markedly abducted, fine-tune rotation.Buttock tenderpoint midway between greater trochanter and coccyx/PSIS line
Lumbar nerve-root decompressionFPR-style: prone, pillow under abdomen, affected leg off table, hip/knee flexed, abduct/flex/compress or traction/gap, hold 4-5 sec, repeat.Course slide names this FPR for lumbar nerve-root pain

LO7 — Pain Generator Differentiation

Pain generatorPatternProvoked byNeurologic deficits?
DiscogenicDeep axial back pain, may refer into buttock/thigh; annular tears can cause chemical radiculitisSitting, flexion, Valsalva/cough in some disc casesNot necessarily unless root involved
Facet jointAxial neck/back pain with referral; lumbar may mimic hip/SIExtension, rotation, facet loading/Kemp'sNo objective root deficit expected
MyofascialTrigger-point referral that may look radicularMuscle load, posture, direct trigger-point pressureNo myotomal/reflex deficit
RadicularDermatomal pain/paresthesia, often distal, below knee for lumbarSpine position, SLR, Spurling, cough/ValsalvaMay have weakness, sensory loss, or reduced DTR

LO12 — OMT Indications and Contraindications

Clinical situationOMT indicated?Reasoning
Somatic dysfunction, mild stable radicular symptoms, normal neuro examOften yes, with cautionGentle indirect/soft-tissue/traction-style care may reduce nociception and improve mechanics
Acute severe radicular pain, no progressive deficitSelective and gentleUse pain-free positions; avoid compressing into symptoms
Progressive weakness, bowel/bladder symptoms, saddle anesthesiaNo routine OMT firstEmergency workup/referral is the priority
Myelopathy signs: hyperreflexia, clonus, Babinski, gait disturbanceContraindication to aggressive OMTPossible cord compression needs imaging and specialty management
Fracture, malignancy, infection, severe osteoporosis, instabilityContraindicated or heavily modifiedRisk of harm exceeds benefit until clarified/managed
Prior spine surgery/fusion/hardwareRequires history/imaging contextConfirm stability; choose gentle non-thrust techniques around, not through, vulnerable segments
